Suggest 20% again? 8.733 ≈ about 97% of mother's income—seems high but he's wealthy (business owner). Alternative: keep 20% (in the middle of the range). Or lower to 18%? The library's practical range for "child support practice" is 15–30%—need–possibility with 2 kids; father's capacity is much higher. Go with 20% = 8.733,33, and note the range. Also note: reinvested profits (not distributed) are not received income; the library says "Pró-labore e lucros distribuídos integram a base quando habituais (pró-labore and distributed profits are included in the base when habitual)"—but since no profits are being distributed, there are no lucros distribuídos to include; note he might be undistributing to avoid support—courts can impute; but the library doesn't say that—don't cite what isn't verified. State as factual observation: since profits are all reinvested, the base includes only pró-labore; flag risk that the other side argues undistributed profits reflect his actual standard of living (label as unverified argument, not a citation). Keep it modest.

This supports communication of appreciation (reinvested profits = fruits of CC 1.660-V per the library; library says "lucros não distribuídos/reinvestidos na constância... comunicam-se"). No change to the 1.100.000 base; date of separation de facto is still unknown—client says no more info. So keep assumption: appraisal value ≈ value at separation. Legal analysis from library: CC 1.659-I excludes sub-rogado (substituted assets); 1.660-V includes fruits. For the house: appreciation attributable to joint funds (renovation)—the library's cc file doesn't have an explicit article (1.659 excludes the asset and sub-rogado; but common-fund improvements create a right to compensation... CC (real law) has articles on benfeitorias but not in the library).
